title: The Retrieval Effectiveness of Web Search Engines: Considering Results Descriptions
extended_summary:
This paper investigates the retrieval effectiveness of five web search engines—Google, Yahoo, MSN, Ask.com, and Seekport—with a particular focus not only on the relevance of returned results but also on the quality of their result descriptions (snippets). The core question is whether Google’s widely perceived superiority is supported by systematic evidence, and whether result descriptions help explain users’ preferences for particular search engines.

The study uses 40 real-life German-language informational queries collected from students at Heinrich-Heine-University Düsseldorf. Participants judged the relevance of anonymized and randomized search results and their descriptions for their own queries. The approach compares engines on multiple retrieval metrics, including proportion of relevant results, micro and macro precision, and several newly proposed measures connecting snippet quality to actual result relevance, such as description-result precision, description-result conformance, description fallout, and description deception.

The population consisted of university students, and the study was conducted in a higher-education research context rather than a school classroom. Data were collected over two days in January 2007. There was no instructional intervention or experimental treatment; instead, the study observed and compared the performance of existing search systems using user relevance judgments. The setting is best characterized as a lab-style evaluation environment using Excel sheets and controlled judging procedures.

The main conclusion is that Google and Yahoo perform similarly on overall relevance of returned results, with no significant difference between them, but Google provides significantly more relevant result descriptions than the other engines. The author argues that this may partly explain why users perceive Google as superior. At the same time, all engines show substantial limitations: overall precision is modest, and misleading descriptions are common. The paper recommends that search engines improve not only result relevance but also the alignment between descriptions and actual result quality.

It contains no K-12 AI writing intervention, no student writing outcomes, and therefore cannot support the requested evidence extraction.
